analysis.one_liner: Bars the VA from letting nurse anesthetists provide anesthesia care without a physician anesthesiologist.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had only two Senate sponsors, died in the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have locked into law that only physician anesthesiologists, not certified registered nurse anesthetists, may have full practice authority over anesthesia care for veterans in VA facilities. It would also have barred the VA from finalizing a 2016 proposed rule that would have let advanced practice nurses work without physician supervision. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Physician anesthesiologists, who would keep sole full-practice authority over VA anesthesia care, and the status quo staffing model they practice under. Supporters say veterans would also benefit from physician-led anesthesia teams.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the VA Secretary from changing anesthesia policy to give full practice authority to any medical professional other than a physician anesthesiologist, and bars the VA from implementing the anesthesia provisions of the 2016 'Advanced Practice Registered Nurses' proposed rule or anything substantially similar.

Supporters frame this as protecting veteran safety by keeping a physician anesthesiologist in charge of anesthesia during surgery, and it preserves short-term emergency orders the VA could still issue for veteran safety during procedures.

analysis.who_pays: The VA health system, which would lose flexibility to staff anesthesia care with nurse anesthetists — a staffing option that is generally less expensive and can expand access, especially in facilities that struggle to recruit physicians. Nurse anesthetists would lose the chance at independent practice in the VA.

drawbacks.text: By statute, the bill would bar the VA from granting full anesthesia practice authority to nurse anesthetists and from finalizing the 2016 rule that would have allowed it, permanently limiting how VA facilities can staff anesthesia care.

Because nurse anesthetists are generally less costly to employ than physician anesthesiologists, the bill could raise VA staffing costs and constrain anesthesia access in VA facilities that cannot recruit enough physicians, with the gains flowing mainly to one physician specialty. Congress would be overriding the VA's own judgment about how to staff its hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety argument — a physician in charge of anesthesia — is a genuine debate in medicine, and keeping VA emergency flexibility is reasonable. But the bill's practical effect is to protect physician anesthesiologists' exclusive role at the VA's expense: it takes staffing and cost decisions out of the hands of the agency that runs the hospitals and could raise costs or limit access, particularly at rural VA facilities. The narrow scope (two sponsors, one committee) suggests even its supporters saw limited urgency.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on June 21, 2023, together with Senator Bill Cassidy, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

The bill would have prohibited the VA from giving full anesthesia practice authority to any provider other than a physician anesthesiologist and from implementing the anesthesia provisions of the 2016 Advanced Practice Registered Nurses proposed rule.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it sat in the Veterans' Affairs Committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nurse anesthetists and the VA, which keep the flexibility to decide how to staff anesthesia care. Physician anesthesiologists did not get the statutory lock-in they sought.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican cosponsor.

for.name: American Society of Anesthesiologists
for.what_they_did: Longstanding national backer of legislation to keep physician anesthesiologists in charge of VA anesthesia care; supported this bill's approach.

against.name: Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Jon Tester
against.what_they_did: As chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote.

against.name: American Association of Nurse Anesthesiology
against.what_they_did: Opposes legislation restricting nurse anesthetist practice authority in the VA and had pushed for the 2016 rule the bill would have killed.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor with one Republican cosponsor out of 49 Senate Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would statutorily guarantee that only physician anesthesiologists hold full practice authority over VA anesthesia, keeping a generally lower-cost alternative (nurse anesthetists practicing independently) off the table and preserving their role and billing position in VA care.

The bill would block nurse anesthetists from ever gaining independent practice authority at the VA, limiting their scope of practice and career advancement; their interest in the bill's failure ran alongside broader access to care for veterans.
The bill would strip the VA of authority to restructure anesthesia staffing, raising its staffing costs while, under supporters' reading, keeping physician oversight of surgery.
